accuracy.evidence: Matches the topic evidence for ages 9 to 11 (order tasks by importance and deadline, identify and manage distractions, focus on one task, estimate task duration) and CASEL self-management. Claims follow the research: task switching carries a measurable reconfiguration cost (Monsell 2003), people underestimate their own task times (Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994), and suppressing a thought tends to bring it back (Wegner 1987). Plan arithmetic is right: 40+15+10+30 = 95 of 120 minutes, and game-first with a 30-minute overrun pushes Spellings to 125 minutes, past 6:30. The 2-minute switch cost and overrun are labelled as a model.

misconceptions.evidence: Tackles the slips children and parents actually report: choosing by mood instead of deadline (challenge 'Whichever I feel like'), 'just one level' first (plan step overrun), believing multitasking is quicker (prediction and challenge 'Yes, two at once'), keeping the phone face down in reach, checking it quickly, pushing a thought away rather than parking it, repeating an optimistic estimate after timing showed otherwise, and leaving a project to the night before.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are specific to time management: a two-bin job sorter by importance and deadline, a timeline planner that runs the evening with a fun-job overrun and shows must-dos cut by the 6:30 line, a focus meter drained by four distraction scenarios with three fixes each, a draggable switch-count knob that redraws work and switch-cost segments, and a guess-time-plan estimator. The shingle gate passed against flag_focus, flag_steps, flag_habit and flag_goal.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is discovered by acting: the evening run proves why fun goes last because the overrun visibly squeezes Spellings, the meter shows which fixes protect focus, the knob shows total time rising by 2 minutes per switch from 18 to 30, and timing reveals the real 32 and 40 minutes so the plan uses evidence rather than a guess.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong answers that the lab then tests: 'Everything still gets done' if the game goes first (the run cuts a must-do past 6:30), and 'Faster: two jobs at once' for maths with messages (the knob shows the total climbing with every switch). The answer is only revealed after the task is completed.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six shuffled challenge questions with twelve distinct wrong-answer tags, each explaining the specific slip: 'One level often becomes three', 'Feelings pick the fun job', 'Too much spare wastes time', 'Pushing a thought away often makes it come back'. Every in-step miss also explains itself, for example the overrun message naming which must-do did not fit.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday jobs (spellings, PE kit, a game level) and passes the learner readability gate; the adult text was shortened to pass the 9.5 grade target and names the curriculum terms prioritise, deadline, urgent, schedule, distraction, task switching and time estimate in plain words.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a rule, a reason or a mistake. There are no intros or recaps. The adult text names six concrete common mistakes, and the family tip gives one specific routine: sticky-note jobs put in order and checked against real times afterwards.

mobile.evidence: All controls are 44 px+ buttons beneath the canvas with drag on the knob and tap-to-place for jobs; text sizes switch with A.narrow. The Show me sequence completes each step in under 5 seconds on desktop and iPhone 13, and screenshots on iPhone and Android show no clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Every action is available as a labelled button (e.g. 'Add Homework, 40 minutes, to the plan'), the canvas has an aria-label and live feedback text, colour is never the only cue because segments carry text labels, and axe reports zero WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light and dark themes.
